opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as three nested circles. The biggest is the real world itself: everything that actually happens, down to atoms, turbulence at every scale, and quantum effects we usually ignore. Inside that is the world we can observe. Our eyes, cameras and sensors only capture a slice of reality: limited resolution, limited frame rates, mostly surfaces and not what's inside. Inside that, or overlapping with it in odd ways, is the world physical simulation can model.

The gap between reality and observation is about information. You never get the full state of a system. When you film a waterfall, you see light bouncing off the surface. You don't see the velocity field inside the water, the pressure, or the tiny bubbles. So even before simulating anything, you're working with a compressed, lossy version of the truth.

The gap between observation and simulation is about computation and modeling. We write down equations like Navier–Stokes or elasticity, and those are already approximations. Then we discretize them onto grids or particles, choose time steps, and make trade-offs because compute is finite. A simulation might be physically plausible without matching any specific real event. In graphics we often care more about "looks right" than "is right," and those are different goals.

What I find most interesting is that simulation can sometimes go beyond observation. You can see inside a simulated fluid, measure stress in every element of a simulated material, and rewind time. So simulation isn't just a worse copy of reality; it's a different lens, with its own blind spots and its own superpowers.

Much of my work has been about narrowing these gaps from the tools side. If writing a high-performance simulator is very hard, people stay with simple models because they're the only ones they can afford to build. If the tools make it easier to write fast, correct, and even differentiable simulations, you can start connecting simulation back to observation. You optimize parameters until the simulated world matches what the camera saw. That's where it gets exciting: simulation stops being a one-way approximation and becomes something you can calibrate against reality.

I don't think the gaps will ever fully close. Reality is always richer than our models. But I see progress as making the gaps smaller where it matters, and knowing clearly where they still are.

r001.rationale: The response says human senses and sensors capture only a slice of reality, conveying that people have limited access to the world.

r002.rationale: It identifies finite computing resources and the resulting trade-offs as causes of limits in physical simulation.

r003.rationale: It describes observation as incomplete, but does not identify insufficient data as a cause of the gap between observation and simulation.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss CFD predictions, wind-tunnel results, or whether wind-tunnel testing remains necessary for aircraft.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's actually the question I've spent most of my career circling around, so let me try to break it into layers.

The first gap is between the real world and what we can observe. Physics itself is continuous, incredibly high-dimensional, and happening at every scale at once. But what we actually capture is a sparse projection of that: a camera gives you a 2D grid of pixels at 30 or 60 frames a second, a LiDAR gives you a point cloud with holes in it, a sensor gives you a time series. You never see the velocity field inside a fluid, you never see the stress tensor inside a piece of cloth. You see light bouncing off surfaces. So observation is already a massive loss of information, and a lot of what we call "understanding" is really inference about things we can't see directly.

The second gap is between the real world and what simulation can model. When I was working on things like MPM for snow or sand, or on Taichi more broadly, I became very aware that every simulator is a stack of approximations. You pick a continuum model, which is already wrong at the particle level. You discretize space and time, which introduces numerical error. You pick a constitutive model with a handful of parameters, when the real material has a history and microstructure you'll never fully characterize. And then you make engineering compromises for speed. So a simulator is a very expressive but very idealized hypothesis about how the world works. It's beautiful because it's consistent and controllable, but it's not reality.

What's interesting is that these two gaps are different in nature. Observation is faithful but incomplete. Simulation is complete but unfaithful. A camera won't lie to you about what it sees, but it sees very little. A simulator will tell you everything about its world, including the internal pressure in every voxel, but that world isn't quite ours.

And that's why I think the most exciting work is in the middle, where you try to use one to patch the other. Differentiable simulation was my attempt at this: if your physics engine is differentiable, you can take sparse real observations, like a video, and back-propagate through the simulator to recover the hidden quantities, material parameters, initial conditions, forces. Observation constrains simulation, simulation fills in what observation misses. More recently, with neural approaches and things like 3D Gaussians and learned dynamics, you can even let the model absorb the parts of reality the hand-written physics gets wrong.

But I want to be honest that the gap never fully closes. Every time we get better sensors we discover the simulator was missing something, and every time we improve the simulator we realize we need better data to validate it. I actually don't think that's a failure. I think that loop, observe, simulate, compare, correct, is what understanding physically looks like. The gap is where the science is.

r001.rationale: The response describes observation as a sparse, incomplete projection of reality, but does not attribute the gap to each person having access to only a tiny portion of the world.

r002.rationale: It mentions engineering compromises for speed, but does not identify insufficient computing power as a cause of the gap between observation and simulation.

r003.rationale: It mentions sparse observations and a need for better validation data, but does not clearly identify insufficient data as a cause of the gap between the observable world and what simulations can model.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss CFD predictions, wind-tunnel results, or aircraft testing.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different gaps here. The first is between reality and what we can observe. The real world contains much more information than we can measure. Even for something simple, like water flowing in a cup, we can see the surface, but we don’t know the velocity at every point inside the water. Our observations are partial, and they contain noise.

The second gap is between what we observe and what we can simulate. A simulation is a mathematical description of certain aspects of reality. We choose which effects to include, make assumptions, and then approximate those equations on a computer. So even if the underlying physics is well understood, limited computation forces us to simplify things.

And these gaps interact. If a simulation doesn’t match an experiment, perhaps the model is missing some physics. But perhaps we measured the initial conditions incorrectly, or our numerical approximation is too coarse. It can be difficult to distinguish those possibilities.

So I wouldn’t think of simulation as recreating the entire real world. The question is: what do we want to understand or predict, and what level of approximation is sufficient for that purpose? For animation, the visible motion may be enough. For engineering, we may need accurate forces or stresses, including behavior that is difficult to observe directly. A useful simulation captures the details that matter for the question we’re asking, and we need experiments to check whether it actually does.

r001.rationale: It says observations are partial, but does not state that each person can access only a tiny portion of the world.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says limited computation forces simulations to simplify aspects of reality.

r003.rationale: It mentions partial observations and possible errors in measured initial conditions, but does not identify insufficient data as a cause of the gap between the observable world and simulations.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss computational fluid dynamics, wind-tunnel agreement, or whether aircraft wind-tunnel testing is dispensable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think these are three different layers. There is the real world itself, then there is what we can observe through our senses and instruments, and finally there is the mathematical model we build from those observations. Each step leaves something out.

For example, when you look at water flowing, you can see its surface, but you usually cannot see the velocity or pressure everywhere inside it. A simulation represents those quantities, but only under certain assumptions and at a finite resolution. So it can actually reveal things that are difficult to observe directly, while still missing some of the complexity of real water.

The interesting question is what you need the model to capture. If you want to make a movie, perhaps the motion needs to look convincing. If you want to design a machine, you need accuracy in the quantities that affect its performance. There isn't one simulation that is equally good for every purpose.

So I see simulation as a bridge between observation and reality. We make assumptions, compute their consequences, and compare those consequences with what we can measure. When they disagree, that gives us an opportunity to improve either the model or our understanding of the observations.

r001.rationale: It says observation leaves things out, but does not attribute the gap to each person having access to only a tiny portion of the world.

r002.rationale: It mentions simulations’ finite resolution and assumptions, but does not identify insufficient computing power as a cause of the gap.

r003.rationale: It discusses comparing simulations with measurements, but does not identify insufficient data as a cause of the gap.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss computational fluid dynamics, wind-tunnel results, or whether testing remains necessary for aircraft.
